paras: The threatened lynching at Newberry, South Carolina, in 1900 involved an unnamed fifteen-year-old Black boy who was jailed at Newberry on a charge of attempted assault on a white girl, Myrtle Farrow, and who, according to a brief press report, "narrowly escaped lynching." The episode is known only from a single sentence in a state-news column of the Anderson Intelligencer of 1 August 1900.

The report gave no date for the alleged offense or for the threat against the boy, saying only that he was in jail at Newberry when the item ran. He was accused of "attempted assault upon Myrtle Farrow, a little white girl." Beyond the statement that he "narrowly escaped lynching," the item described no mob, no gathering at the jail, and no action by officers, and it did not say whether the threat came during his capture or after he was jailed.
No report of a trial, a sentence, or any further threat against the boy was found in the coverage, and his name does not appear.

The Anderson Intelligencer ran the item among unrelated state news, between a notice of a Holiness Association meeting and a report of a magistrate's shooting at Ulmer. It stated the accusation without qualification, named no source, and referred to the boy as "the young coon." No other white newspaper and no Black newspaper was found to have reported the episode in August or September 1900.

accounts.label: State news item
accounts.gist: A fifteen-year-old Black boy was in jail at Newberry for attempted assault on a little white girl and narrowly escaped lynching.

framing.detail: No condemnation of the lynching threat; the item treats the accusation as established and uses the slur 'the young coon'.
